32:1: Abu Jaafar said: The explanation of the interpretation of His statement Alif, Lam, Meem has been given sufficiently. Abu Ja`far said: The translators of the Qur’an differed in their interpretation of the words of God Almighty: Alif, Lam, Meem. Some of them said: It is one of the names of the Qur’an. Those who said that mentioned: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement: Alif, Lam, Meem, he said: It is one of the names of the Qur’an. Al-Muthanna bin Ibrahim Al-Amili told me: Abu Hudhayfah Musa bin Mas`ud told us: Shabl told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: Alif, Lam, Meem is one of the names of the Qur’an. Al-Qasim bin Al-Hasan told us: Al-Hussein bin Dawud told us: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Alif, Lam, Meem is one of the names of the Qur’an. Some of them said: They are opening verses with which God opens the Quran. Those who said this were: Harun ibn Idris al-Asamm al-Kufi told me: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Maharbi told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: Alif, Lam, Meem are opening verses with which God opens the Qur’an. Ahmad bin Hazim Al-Ghafari told us: Abu Naim told us: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: Alif, Lam, Meem are opening letters. Al-Muthanna bin Ibrahim told me: Ishaq bin Al-Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Yahya bin Adam, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Ibn Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: Alif, Lam, Meem, Alif, Muḥammad, and Sad are the opening letters with which God began. Al-Qasim bin Al-Hasan told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, like the hadith of Harun bin Idris. Others said: It is the name of the Surah. Those who said this are: Yunus bin Abdul A’la told me, he said: Abdullah bin Wahb told us, he said: I asked Abdul Rahman bin Zaid bin Aslam about the words of God: “Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book,” and “Alif, Lam, Meem. This is a revelation,” and “Alif, Lam, Meem. That is the name of the chapters.” He said: My father said: They are only the names of the chapters. Some of them said: It is the greatest name of God. Those who said this are: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi told us: Shu’bah told us: I asked al-Suddi about Ha Meem, “Ta Seen Meem,” and Alif Lam Meem. He said: Ibn Abbas said: They are the greatest name of God. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us: Abu al-Nu’man told us: Shu’bah told us, on the authority of Ismail al-Suddi, on the authority of Murrah al-Hamadani, who said: Abdullah said: He mentioned something similar. Al-Muthanna told me: Ishaq bin Al-Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ubaidullah bin Musa, on the authority of Ismail, on the authority of Al-Sha’bi, who said: The openings of the surahs are among the names of God. Some of them said: It is an oath by which God swears, and it is one of His names. Those who said this were: Yahya bin Othman bin Saleh Al-Sahmi told me, he said: Abdullah bin Saleh told us, he said: Muawiyah bin Saleh told me, on the authority of Ali bin Abi Talha, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: It is an oath by which God swears, and it is one of the names of God. Yaqub bin Ibrahim told us: Ibn Ulayyah told us: Khalid Al-Hadha’ told us, on the authority of Ikrimah, who said: Alif, Lam, Meem is an oath. Some of them said: It is a collection of letters separated from nouns and verbs, each letter having a meaning different from the meaning of the other letter. Those who said this are: Abu Kurayb told us, he said: Waki` told us, and Sufyan ibn Waki` told us, he said: My father told us, on the authority of Sharik, on the authority of Ata` ibn al-Sa`ib, on the authority of Abu al-Dhaha, on the authority of Ibn Abbas: Alif, Lam, Meem. He said: I, God, know best. It was narrated on the authority of Abu Ubaid, who said: Abu Al-Yaqzan narrated to us, on the authority of Ata’ bin Al-Sa’ib, on the authority of Sa’id bin Jubayr, who said: His statement, Alif, Lam, Meem, he said: I, God, know best. Musa bin Harun Al-Hamdani told me: Amr bin Hammad Al-Qannad told us: Asbat bin Nasr told us, on the authority of Ismail Al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, on the authority of Abu Malik, and on the authority of Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and on the authority of Murrah Al-Hamdani, on the authority of Ibn Masoud, and on the authority of some of the companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: Alif, Lam, Meem. He said: As for Alif, Lam, Meem, it is a letter derived from the letters of the spelling of the names of God, may His praise be exalted. Muhammad ibn Muammar told us: Abbas ibn Ziyad al-Bahili told us: Shu’bah told us, on the authority of Abu Bishr, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding His statement: Alif, Lam, Meem, “Ha, Meem,” and Nun, he said: It is a disconnected noun. Some of them said that they are letters of the alphabet that were placed. Those who said that were mentioned: It was narrated on the authority of Mansur ibn Abi Nuwayrah, who said: Abu Saeed al-Mu'addab narrated to us, on the authority of Khasif, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: The opening letters of all the surahs, Qaf, "Sad, Ha Meem, Ta Seen Meem, Alif Lam Ra," and others, are a fabricated spelling. Some of them said: They are letters, each of which includes various different meanings. Those who said that were mentioned: Al-Muthanna bin Ibrahim Al-Tabari told me: Ishaq bin Al-Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Abdullah bin Abi Jaafar Al-Razi, who said: My father told me, on the authority of Al-Rabi bin Anas, regarding the statement of God, the Most High: Alif, Lam, Meem, he said: These letters, from the twenty-nine letters, are spoken by all tongues. There is not a letter among them that is not a key to one of His names. There is not a letter among them that is not related to His favors and trials, and there is not a letter among them that is not related to the duration of a people and their appointed times. Jesus, son of Mary, said: And it is strange that they speak of His names and live in His provision, so how can they deny Him? He said: The Alif is the key to His name: God, the Lam is the key to His name: Latif, and the Mim is the key to His name: Majeed. The Alif is the favors of God, the Lam is His kindness, and the Mim is His glory. The Alif is years, the Lam is thirty years, and the Mim is forty years. Ibn Hamid told us: Hakam told us, on the authority of Abu Ja`far, on the authority of Al-Rabi`, something similar. Some of them said: These are letters from the abjad numeral system. We were reluctant to mention the one who narrated this, as the one who narrated it was someone whose narration and transmission were not reliable. A similar narration has already been reported from Al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Some of them said: Every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur’an is its openings. As for the Arabists, they differed about the meaning of that. Some of them said: They are letters from the alphabetical letters, and mentioning what was mentioned of them at the beginnings of the surahs dispensed with mentioning the rest of them, which are the completion of the twenty-eight letters, just as the informant dispensed with mentioning what he reported that there are twenty-eight letters in the alphabet by mentioning A B T Th, without mentioning the rest of its letters, which are the completion of the twenty-eight. He said: Therefore, that book was raised, because the meaning of the speech is: Alif, Lam, and Mim are from the separate letters, that is the book which I have revealed to you all together, there is no doubt about it. If someone says: A B T Th has become like a noun in the letters of the alphabet, just as Al-Hamd was the name of the Opening of the Book. It was said to him: Since it was permissible for a speaker to say: My son is in Ṭā Ḍaḥ, and it was known from his saying that if he said it that he wanted to report about his son that he was in the disconnected letters, it was known from that that Ṭā Ḍaḥdoes not have a name, even if that was more effective in mentioning than the rest of them. He said: The difference between mentioning the letters of the alphabet in the openings of the surahs is that they are mentioned at their beginnings differently, and they are mentioned when they are mentioned at their beginnings, which are A B T Th, together, in order to separate the report about them if what is meant by mentioning what is mentioned from them differently is to indicate connected speech and if what is meant by mentioning what is mentioned from them together is to indicate the separate letters specifically. And they cited as evidence for the permissibility of the saying of the speaker: My son in T Z and the like, from the report about it that it is in the letters of the alphabet, and that this is from his saying in the statement that it takes the place of his saying: My son in A B T Th in the rajaz of some of the rajaz poets of Banu Asad: When I saw her matter in Hatti and I joked about her lying and flattery I took from her the horns of the Shamat, and she has not left me with her and her giving Even the head was covered with blood He claimed that he meant by that the report about the woman that she was in Abu Jad, so he made his statement: When I saw her matter in Hatti, in place of his report about her that she was in Abu Jad, since that was from his statement, indicating to his listener what his statement: When I saw her matter in Abu Jad indicates to him. Others said: Rather, it was started with this at the beginning of the surahs to open the ears of the polytheists to listening to it, as they had advised each other to turn away from the Qur’an, so that when they listened to it, the composition of it would be recited to them. Some of them said: The letters that open the Surahs are letters with which God opens His speech. If it is said: Is there anything in the Qur’an that has no meaning? It was said: The meaning of this is that he began with it to indicate that the surah before it had ended, and that he had begun another, so he made this a sign of the break between them. This is in the speech of the Arabs, when a man among them recites poetry and says: But, a town whose people are not human He says: No, it did not stir up sorrows and grief But it is not from the verse and is not counted in its meter, but it is used to interrupt a sentence and start another. Abu Jaafar said: Each of the statements made by those whose statement we have described in this regard has a known basis. As for those who said: Alif, Lam, Meem is one of the names of the Qur’an, there are two aspects to their statement: One: That they meant that "Alif, Lam, Meem is the name of the Qur'an, just as Al-Furqan" is its name. If the meaning of the speaker is thus, then the interpretation of his statement, "Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book," is to mean an oath. It is as if he said: By the Qur'an, this Book, there is no doubt about it. The other of them: That they meant that it is one of the names of the surah by which it is known, just as all other things are known by their names which have signs by which they are known. So the listener understands from the speaker saying: Today I read Al-Muddaththir and Al-Nun, meaning the surahs that he read from the surahs of the Qur’an, just as he understands from him if he says: Today I met Amr and Zayd, and they know by Zayd and Amr what he met from the people. If the meaning of this is unclear to someone, he may say: How can this be so, when there are a number of surahs similar to alif, lam, meem and alif, lam-ra in the Qur’an? Names are only indicators if they distinguish between people, but if they are not distinguishing, then they are not indicators. It has been said: Although the names have become, due to the commonality of many people in one of them, not distinctive except by other meanings with it, such as adding the relation of the named to it, or its description or attribute, in a way that distinguishes it from other forms of it, they were initially established for distinction, no doubt. Then, when there is a need for the meanings that distinguish between those named by them. Likewise, in the names of the surahs, each name, according to the one who said this, was made an indication of the surah named by it. So, since the named shares in it other surahs of the Qur’an, the one reporting a surah from it needed to add to its name the named by it something that would differentiate the hearer between reporting about it and others, of a description, attribute, or other than that. So the one reporting about himself says that he recited Surat Al-Baqarah, if he calls it by its name, which is Alif, Lam, Meem: I read Alif, Lam, Meem, Al-Baqarah. And in Al Imran 3:I read Alif, Lam, Meem, Al Imran. And “Alif, Lam, Meem. That is the Book.” "And "And, 'Alif, Lam, Mim. God, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining." It is as if he wanted to inform about two men, each of whose name was Amr, except that one of them was Tamimi and the other Azdi, he would have to say to the one he wanted to inform about them: I met Amr al-Tamimi and Amr al-Azdi, since there is no difference between them and others who share their names, except their lineage. This is also the case with those who interpret the disconnected letters as names of surahs. As for those who said: These are openings with which God Almighty begins His speech, they directed that to something similar to the meaning we narrated from the one we narrated that from among the Arabs, that he said: These are evidence of the end of a surah and the beginning of another, and a sign of the interruption of what is between them, just as you made rather at the beginning of a poem an indication of the beginning of it and the end of another before it. Just as we mentioned about the Arabs, when they wanted to begin reciting a poem, they would say: Rather, what stirred up sorrows and grief had been grief. But it is not from the house nor is it included in its meter, but it is used to indicate the end of one speech and the beginning of another. As for those who said: These are disconnected letters, some of which are names of God Almighty, and some of which are attributes of Him, and each letter has a meaning other than the meaning of the other letter, then they interpreted this in a manner similar to the poet’s saying: We said to her: Stand for us. She said: Stand. Don't think that we forgot to stand. Meaning by his saying: Qalata Qaf, she said: I have stopped. So by making the Qaf pronounced from Waqafa, she indicated what she meant by the completion of the word in which she stopped. So they diverted his saying Alif, Lam, Meem and the like to something like this meaning. Some of them said: The Alif is the Alif of Ana, the Lam is the Lam of God, and the Meem is the Meem of A’lam, and each letter of them indicates a complete word. They said: So the sum of these disconnected letters, if they appear with each letter of them, completes the letters of the word, Ana, God A’lam. They said: And likewise all that is at the beginning of the chapters of the Qur’an from that, so based on this meaning and this interpretation, they said: It is widespread and apparent in the speech of the Arabs that the speaker among them reduces letters from the word, if what remains indicates what was deleted from it and adds to it what is not from it, if the addition does not confuse its meaning to its listener, like their deletion in the reduction of the Tha’ from Harith, so they say Ya Har, and from Malik the Kaf, so they say Ya Mal, and the like, and like the saying of their rajaz poet: What is wrong with the oppressed? How can he not save his skin if he does not? As if he wanted to say: If he does such and such, he was satisfied with the letter ya from yaf’ala, and as another of them said: Good things come to you, and evil things come to you. He wants: evil. I don't want evil unless you He wants: unless you wish, so he was satisfied with the ta’ and the fa’ in both words, from the rest of their letters, and other similar examples that would take too long to cover in the book. And as Yaqub bin Ibrahim told me, he said: Ibn Ulayyah told us, on the authority of Ayoub and Ibn Awn, on the authority of Muhammad, he said: When Yazid bin Muawiyah died, Abda said to me: I do not see it except as a trial, so flee from your estate and join your family. I said: What do you command me? He said: I would prefer for you to... Ayoub and Ibn Awn said, with his hand under his right cheek, describing lying down until you see a matter that you recognize. Abu Ja`far said: He meant by Ṭadtaji`u, so he sufficed with the Ṭadtaji`u from Ṭadtaji`u. And as the other said in the addition to the statement, in the manner that I described: I say, when you fell on the hump, O my camel, you have not traveled far He wants: all of it, and as the other said: My shape and your shape are different, so stick to the short ones and lower your whites So he added a letter Ḍād, but it is not in the word. They said: Likewise, what is missing from the complete letters of each of these words that we mentioned is the completion of the letters Alif-Lam-Meem and its counterparts is similar to what is missing from the speech that we narrated from the Arabs in their poetry and speech. As for those who said: Every letter of alif-laam-meem and its counterparts indicates various meanings, like what we mentioned from Ar-Rabi’ ibn Anas, they explained that to the same interpretation as he explained to him who said: It is based on the interpretation God knows best, in that every letter of it is some of the letters of a complete word, and its indication of its completeness suffices without mentioning its completeness, even though they disagreed with him regarding every letter of that: Is it from the word that the proponents of the first opinion claimed it was from, or from another one? They said: Rather, the alif of alif-laam-meem is from various words, and it indicates the meanings of all of that and its completeness. They said: Each letter of that was isolated, and was limited by it to completing the letters of the word, because if all of the letters of the word were made clear, the word that is made clear, in which some of these disconnected letters are some, would only indicate one meaning, not two meanings or more than that. They said: Since there is no indication in that, if all of them were made clear, except for their meaning, which is a single meaning, and since God, the Most High, intended to indicate with each letter many meanings for one thing, it is not permissible except to isolate the letter indicating those meanings, so that those addressed by it know that God, the Mighty and Sublime, did not intend to intend one meaning and indicate one thing with what He addressed them with, and that He only intended to indicate many things with it. They said: The Alif in Alif, Lam, Meem implies many meanings, including the completion of the name of the Lord, which is God, and the completion of the name of God’s blessings, which are His favors, and the indication that the lifespan of a people is one year, since the Alif in the abjad system is one. The Lam implies the completion of the name of God, which is Latif, and the completion of the name of His bounty, which is Lutf, and the indication that the lifespan of a people is thirty years. The Mim implies the completion of the name of God, which is Majestic, and the completion of the name of His Greatness, which is Majestic, and the indication that the lifespan of a people is forty years. The meaning of the speech, according to the interpretation of those who say the first opinion, is that God, may He be glorified and exalted, began His speech by describing Himself as the All-Knowing from whom nothing is hidden, and He made that a method for His servants to follow at the beginning of their sermons, letters, and affairs, and a test from Him for them so that they may deserve a great reward in the abode of recompense, just as He began with Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and Praise be to God, who created the heavens and the earth (al-An’am 6:1), and other similar surahs whose openings He made praise of Himself, and just as He made the openings of some of them glorifying and venerating Himself with praise, as He, may He be glorified and exalted, said: Glory be to Him who took His servant by night (al-Isra’ 17:1), and other similar surahs of the Qur’an, the openings of some of which He made praising Himself, the openings of some of which glorifying Him, and the openings of some of which glorifying and sanctifying Him. Likewise, He made the keys to the other surahs, which begin with some letters of the alphabet, praises of Himself, sometimes with knowledge, sometimes with justice and fairness, and sometimes with generosity and kindness, in brief and concise terms, then the matters are summarized after that. According to this interpretation, the alif, lam, and mim in the places of the nominative case should be raised by each other, without his saying that book, and that book would be a predicate subject separate from the meaning of alif, lam, mim. Likewise, that in the interpretation of the statement of the one who says this second statement, is raised by each other, even if its meaning is different from the meaning of the statement of the one who says the first statement. As for those who said: They are letters from the letters of the abjad calculation without any meanings that contradict that, they said: We do not know of any meaning for the disconnected letters that can be understood other than the abjad calculation, and other than the spelling of the saying of the speaker: Alif, Lam, Meem. They said: It is not permissible for God, the Most High, to address His servants except in a way that they understand and comprehend. Since that is the case and His saying Alif, Lam, Meem does not have a rational face that could be directed to it, except one of the two faces that we mentioned, then one of its faces is invalidated, which is that it is intended by it to spell Alif, Lam, Meem. It is correct and proven that it is intended by it to mean the second face, which is the abjad calculation, because the saying of the speaker: Alif, Lam, Meem cannot be followed by the statement That is the Book, because the meaning of the statement is impossible and goes beyond reason, if “Alif, Lam, Meem. That is the Book” follows it. They also argued for their statement with the following: Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi narrated to us: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me: al-Kalbi narrated to me, on the authority of Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of Jabir ibn Abdullah ibn Ri’ab, who said: “Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab passed by the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, while he was reciting the opening verse of Surat al-Baqarah 2:‘Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book about which there is no doubt.’ So his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab from the Jews came and said: ‘By God, you know that I heard Muhammad reciting, in what God, the Almighty, revealed to him, ‘Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book.’ They said: Did you hear it? He said: ‘Yes!’ So Huyayy ibn Akhtab walked with those Jews to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and they said: ‘O Muhammad, was it not mentioned to us that you recite, in what was revealed to you, ‘Alif, Lam, Meem. This is the Book.’ The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Yes.’ They said: ‘Did Gabriel bring this to you from God?’ He said: ‘Yes.’ They said: God, the Almighty, has sent prophets before you, and we do not know of any prophet among them who explained what…’” His reign was prolonged and his nation did not eat except you! So Huyayy ibn Akhtab said, and he turned to those who were with him and said to them: The Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, and the Mim is forty, so that is seventy-one years. Will you enter the religion of a prophet whose reign and nation did not eat except for seventy-one years? He said: Then he turned to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: O Muhammad, is there anything else with this? He said: Yes. He said: What? He said: Alif-Lam-Meem. He said: This is heavier and longer. The Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, the Mim is forty, and the Sad is ninety, so that is one hundred and sixty-one years. Is there anything else with this, O Muhammad? He said: Yes. He said: What? He said: Alif-Lam-Ra. He said: By God, this is heavier and longer. The Alif is one, the Lam is thirty, and the Ra is two hundred, so that is two hundred and thirty-one years. He said: Is there anything else with this, O Muhammad? He said: Yes, al-murr. He said: By God, this is heavier and longer. The alif is one, the lam is thirty, the mim is forty, and the ra is two hundred. This is two hundred and seventy-one years. Then he said: Your matter has become so confusing to us, O Muhammad, that we do not know whether you have been given a little or a lot. Then they got up from him. Abu Yasir said to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab and the rabbis who were with him: How do you know? Perhaps he has gathered all of this for Muhammad: seventy-one, sixty-one and one hundred, two hundred and thirty-one, two hundred and seventy-one. That is seven hundred and thirty-four years! They said: His matter has become confusing to us! They claim that these verses were revealed about them: “It is He who has sent down to you, [O Muhammad], the Book. In it are verses that are precise - they are the foundation of the Book - and others unspecific.” (Al Imran 3:7) They said: This report clearly proves the correctness of what we have said about this interpretation, and the corruption of what our opponents have said about it. The correct statement in my opinion about the interpretation of the keys to the Surahs, which are the letters of the alphabet, is that God, the Most High, made them separate letters and did not connect some of them to others, making them like all other speech with connected letters, because He, the Most High, intended by His wording to indicate with each letter many meanings, not just one meaning, as Ar-Rabi’ ibn Anas said. Even though Ar-Rabi’ limited it to three meanings, without anything more than that. The correct interpretation of this, in my opinion, is that each letter of it contains what Al-Rabi’ said, and what all other commentators have said about it, except for what I mentioned from the people of Arabic who I mentioned: that he directed the interpretation of this to that they are letters of the alphabet. Mentioning what he mentioned of it in the keys to the surahs suffices, without mentioning the rest of the twenty-eight letters of the alphabet, by interpreting: that these letters, that book, are collected, there is no doubt about it, for it is a false and corrupt statement, as it departs from the statements of all the companions and followers and those who came after them from the dissenters of the people of interpretation and exegesis. So it is sufficient to indicate his error, the testimony of the proof against him of the error, with the invalidation of the one who said that, as we have narrated from him, when he turned to explaining the raising of that book by saying once that each one of them is raised by its companion, and another time that it is raised by the referent of what he mentioned in his saying there is no doubt about it, and once by his saying a guidance for the righteous. This is an omission from him, based on his statement that alif, lam, mim is the subject of that book, and a departure from the statement he claimed in the interpretation of “alif, lam, mim. That book,” and that the interpretation of that is: these letters are that book. If someone were to say to us: How can one letter be comprehensive in indicating many different meanings? It was said: Just as it is possible for a single word to include many different meanings, such as their saying for a group of al-Nas 114:a nation, and for a particular moment in time: a nation, and for a devout and obedient man: a nation, and for religion and creed: a groan. And like their saying for recompense and retaliation: a religion, and for authority and obedience: a religion, and for humiliation: a religion, and for accountability: a religion, and there are many similar things that would take a long time to list, as speech is made with one word, and it includes many meanings. And likewise the statement of God, may He be praised: Alif, Lam, Meem, “Alif, Lam, Ra,” Alif, Lam, Meem, and what is similar to that from the letters of the alphabet which are the opening letters of the surahs, each letter of which denotes various meanings, encompassing all of them from the names and attributes of God, the Almighty, as the commentators have said from the sayings we have mentioned. And they are, however, the opening letters of the surahs, as those who have said so have said. And the fact that these are from the letters of the names and attributes of God, may He be praised, does not prevent them from being opening letters for the surahs. Because God, may He be glorified and praised, has opened many chapters of the Qur’an with praise and thanks to Himself, and many of them with glorification and exaltation of Him, so it is not impossible that some of them begin with an oath by Him. As for the ones whose opening letters begin with the letters of the alphabet, one of the meanings of their opening letters is that they are the opening letters of the chapters of the Qur’an. They are among what God swore by, because one of their meanings is that they are letters of the names and attributes of God, the Most High, as we have explained previously. There is no doubt that the meaning of swearing by God, His names and attributes is correct. They are among the letters of the abjad system. They are symbols and names for the chapters that begin with them. This encompasses the meanings of all that we have described, from what we have explained, from its aspects. Because if God, the Most High, had intended by this, or part of it, to indicate a single meaning from what it could bear, without all other meanings, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, would have made that clear to them. This is because God, the Most High, only revealed His Book to His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, to clarify to them what they differed about. And in the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, not explaining that, that some of its interpretations are intended by it and not others, is the clearest evidence that it is intended by all of its aspects for which it is possible. It was not impossible in the mind for any of them to be from its interpretation and meaning, just as it was not impossible for the many meanings of one word to come together, in one expression, in one statement. Whoever rejects what we have said about this should be asked about the difference between this and other letters that have a single pronunciation, yet contain many different meanings, such as nation, religion, and similar nouns and verbs. He will not say anything about one of these without necessarily saying the same thing about the other. Likewise, anyone who interprets any of these things in a way that is different from the other ways we have described should be asked about the proof for his claim, from the way that must be accepted. Then he should counter with the statement of his opponent on this matter, and ask about the difference between them: from the origin, or from what the origin indicates. So he will not say one statement without requiring the same in the other. As for the grammarians who claimed that this is similar to the saying of the poet: Rather, what stirred up sorrows and grief had been grief. And that it has no meaning, but rather it is an addition to the speech whose meaning is to throw it away, so he made a mistake in many ways: One of them is that he described God Almighty as having addressed the Arabs in a language other than their own, nor in the language of any human being. Although the Arabs used to begin their poetry with bal, it is known that they never began any of their speech with alif, lam, meem, “alif, ra,” or alif, mas, in the sense of beginning it with bal. And since that was not part of their beginning, and God Almighty only addressed them with what He addressed them from the Qur’an, with what they knew of their languages and what they used among themselves of their speech, in every verse, then there is no doubt that the path of what we have described of the letters of the alphabet, with which the beginnings of the surahs, which are openings, is the path of the rest of the Qur’an, in that He did not deviate with them from the languages they knew and used among themselves in their speech. Because if this was deviated from the path of their languages and logic, it would be outside the meaning of clarification with which God, the Almighty, described the Qur’an, when He, the Most High, said: The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue (Ash-Shu’ara’: 193-195). How can something be made clear that no one in the world can comprehend or understand, according to the statement of the one who said this statement, and that is not known in the language of any of the created beings, according to his statement? And in God’s statement that it is a clear Arabic, there is what belies this statement, and indicates that the Arabs were knowledgeable about it, and it is clear to them. This is one of the aspects of his error. The second aspect of his error in this regard is that by attributing it to God, the Most High, He addressed His servants with something that has no benefit or meaning for them, through speech in which it is the same to address them with it or not to address them with it. This is by attributing the futility that is denied in the words of all monotheists about God to God, the Most High. The third aspect of his error is that bal in the speech of the Arabs has an interpretation and meaning, and that they include it in their speech to return to a statement that has already been completed, like their saying: It was not your brother who came to me, but rather your father, and I did not see Omar, but rather Abdullah, and similar statements, as A’sha of Banu Tha’labah said: And I will drink eight, eight, thirteen, two, and four. He continued his speech until he said: In the sitting, and the goodness of his arms is like a balloon that hits me like a finger Then he said: Rather, count this, in another verse, and mention a young man of generous nature, the most wonderful. It is as if he said: Leave this and take up another style of poetry. Rather, it only comes in the speech of the Arabs in this manner of speech. As for opening their speech with a beginning meaning of length and deletion, without indicating a meaning, that is something that we do not know of anyone who has claimed from the people of knowledge of the Arabic language and its logic, except for the one whose statement you mentioned. So that would be a principle by which the letters of the alphabet, which are the openings of the chapters of the Qur’an that were opened with it, could be likened if they were similar to it, so how is it that it is far from resembling it?
32:2: And His statement, The revelation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, God Almighty says: The revelation of the Book that was sent down to Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, about which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds: He says: from the Lord of the two heavy burdens: the jinn and mankind. Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement, “Alif, Lam, Meem. The revelation of the Book about which there is no doubt,” there is no doubt about it. Rather, the meaning of the statement is that this Qur’an that was sent down to Muhammad is undoubtedly from God, and it is not poetry or the rhyme of a soothsayer, nor is it something that Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, invented. Rather, the Most High denied with that the statement of those who said, ‘Legends of the former peoples which he wrote down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening.’ Al-Furqan 25:5 and the statement of those who said, This is not but a lie he invented, and another people aided him in it. Al-Furqan 25:4
32:3: And His statement, Or do they say, 'He invented it?' God Almighty says, the polytheists say, Muhammad invented this book of his own accord and you deny it. This am is a confirmation. We have already explained in more than one place in our book that when the Arabs interrogate in a sentence that has already been mentioned, they ask with am. Some of them have claimed that the meaning of this is, And they say. He said, Aam means and, meaning rather in a place like this. Then God Almighty proved them wrong and said, "It is not as you claim and say, that Muhammad invented it. Rather, it is the truth and the truth from your Lord, O Muhammad. He sent it down to you, so that you may warn a people of the punishment and might of God, that He would befall them for their disbelief in Him." No warner came to them before you, He says, There did not come to these people to whom your Lord sent you, O Muhammad, and they are his people from Quraysh, a warner to warn them of the punishment of God for their disbelief before you. His saying, Perhaps they will be guided, means: So that you may find out the path of truth, so that they may know it and believe in it. And the people of interpretation said the same as what we said in interpreting that. Who said that? Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada: That you may warn a people to whom no warner came before you, that they may be guided. He said: They were an illiterate nation, and no warner came to them before Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.
32:4: God Almighty says: The One to be worshipped, O people, who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them, in six days, then He established Himself on His throne on the seventh day after creating the heavens and the earth and what is between them. As Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, God is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days and then established Himself on the Throne on the seventh day, he says: You, O people, have no god except the One who did this deed and created this wondrous creation in six days. And His statement, You have no protector or intercessor besides Him, means: O people, you have no protector or intercessor besides Him to take care of your affairs and support you against Him if He intends to harm you, nor an intercessor to intercede for you with Him if He punishes you for your disobedience to Him. He says: So take Him as a protector, and seek help with Him and His obedience in your affairs, for He will protect you if He intends to protect you from those who intend to harm you, and no one will be able to repel Him from what He intends for you, because no one can subdue Him, and no one can overcome Him. Do you not remember? God Almighty says: Will you not consider and reflect, O people, and learn that you have no protector or intercessor besides Him, so single out divinity for Him, devote worship to Him alone, and abandon all rivals and gods besides Him.
32:5: God Almighty says: God is the One who manages the affairs of His creation from the heavens to the earth, then it ascends to Him. The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of His statement, Then it will ascend to Him in a Day the extent of which is a thousand years of those which you count. Some of them said: Its meaning is that the command descends from the heaven to the earth, and ascends from the earth to the heaven in a single day, the extent of which is a thousand years of those which you count of the days of this world, because the distance between the earth and the heaven is five hundred years, and the distance between the heaven and the earth is the same, so that is a thousand years. Who said that? Ibn Hamid told us: Hakam told us, on the authority of Amr ibn Maruf, on the authority of Laith, on the authority of Mujahid: On a day the measure of which is a thousand years. He meant by that the descent of the command from heaven to earth, and from earth to heaven in one day, the measure of which is a thousand years, because the distance between heaven and earth is a journey of five hundred years. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada: He directs the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a Day of your days the extent of which is a thousand years of those which you count. He says: The extent of His journey on that Day is a thousand years of those which you count of your days of the days of this world, five hundred years of His descent and five hundred years of His ascent, so that is a thousand years. Ibn Wakee’ told us: Abu Mu’awiyah told us, on the authority of Juwaybir, on the authority of Ad-Dahhak: Then it will ascend to Him in a Day the extent of which will be a thousand years of those which you count. He said: The angels ascend to the heavens, then they will descend in one of your days, which is a journey of a thousand years. He said: My father told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Samak, on the authority of Ikrimah, A thousand years of what you count. He said: Of the days of this world. Hanad bin Al-Sarri told us: Abu Al-Ahwas told us, on the authority of Abu Al-Harith, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding His statement, He directs the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it will ascend to Him in a day of your days, a journey between the heaven and the earth of five hundred years. It was reported on the authority of Abd al-Razzaq, who said: Muammar informed us, on the authority of Qatada, who said: Matters descend and ascend from the heavens to the earth in one day, the length of which is a thousand years, five hundred until it descends, and five hundred until it ascends. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: He manages the matter from heaven to earth, then it ascends to Him on one of the six days in which God created creation. The length of that day is a thousand years of what you count of your days. Who said that? Ibn Hamid told us: Hakam told us, on the authority of Anbasa, on the authority of Samak, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas: A thousand years of what you count. He said: That is the length of a journey. His statement: Like a thousand years of what you count. (al-Hajj 22:47) He said: He created the heavens and the earth in six days, and each day of these is like a thousand years of what you count. Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told us, on the authority of Israel, on the authority of Samak, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas: On a Day the measure of which is a thousand years of those which you count. He said: The six days in which God created the heavens and the earth. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Ad-Dahhak say regarding His statement, On a Day the measure of which is a thousand years of those which you count, meaning this day is one of the six days in which God created the heavens and the earth and everything between them. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: He manages the matter from heaven to earth through the angels, then the angels ascend to Him, in a day whose length is a thousand years of the days of this world. Who said that? Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, Then he will ascend to Him in a Day the length of which will be a thousand years, he said: This is in this world, the angels will ascend to Him in a Day the length of which will be a thousand years. Ibn Wakee’ told us: Ghundar told us, on the authority of Shu’bah, on the authority of Samak, on the authority of Ikrimah: On a Day the measure of which is a thousand years. He said: The distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of a thousand years of what you count as days of the Hereafter. Ibn Al-Muthanna told us: Muhammad Ibn Ja`far told us: Shu`bah told us, on the authority of Samak, on the authority of `Ikrimah, that he said regarding this verse, It will ascend to Him in a Day the extent of which will be a thousand years of those which you count. He said: The distance between the heaven and the earth is a journey of a thousand years. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: He manages the matter from heaven to earth in a day, the duration of which is a thousand years of what you count of the days of this world, then that management which He managed ascends to Him. Who said that? It was reported on the authority of Hajjaj, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, that he said: The affair of everything is decreed to the angels for a thousand years, and then likewise until a thousand years have passed, then the affair of everything is decreed for a thousand, and then likewise forever. He said: A day whose duration was, he said: The day is when it is said to what is decreed to the angels for a thousand years, Be, and it is. But He called it a day, He called it as we have explained. All of that is on the authority of Mujahid. He said: And His statement: {Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of those which you count.} (al-Hajj 22:47) is killed: it is the same. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: He manages the matter from heaven to earth, then it ascends to God in a day the length of which is a thousand years, the length of the ascension is a thousand years of what you count. Who said that? Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His statement, Then he will ascend to Him in a Day the extent of which will be a thousand years of those which you count, some of the people of knowledge said, the extent of the distance between the earth when he ascends to Him until his ascension reaches a thousand years, this is the extent of that ascension on that day when he ascends on it. The first and most correct of the sayings on this matter, in my opinion, is the saying of the one who said: Its meaning is: He directs the affair from the heavens to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a day, the length of that day in the ascension of that affair to Him and its descent to the earth is a thousand years of what you count of your days, five hundred in the descent and five hundred in the ascent, because that is the most obvious of its meanings and the most similar to the apparent meaning of the revelation.
32:6: God Almighty says: This One who does what I have described to you in these verses, is the Knower of the Unseen, meaning the Knower of what is hidden from your sight, O people, so you do not see it of what the hearts conceal and the souls conceal, and what has not yet been of what is to come, and the witnessed: meaning what the eyes have witnessed, seen and witnessed and what is to come. The Almighty says: The Severe in His vengeance upon whoever disbelieved in Him and associated others with Him, and denied His Messengers. The Merciful to whoever repents from his misguidance and returns to belief in Him and in His Messenger, and acts in obedience to Him, that He will punish him after repentance. And His statement, Who has perfected everything He created, the reciters differed in their recitation of this. Some reciters from Mecca, Medina, and Basra recited it He has perfected everything He created with a sukoon on the lam. Some Medinans and most of the Kufians recited it He has perfected everything He created with a fatha on the lam. The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is: They are two well-known readings, each of which has been recited by scholars of the Qur’an, and they both have a correct meaning. This is because God perfected His creation and perfected everything He created, so whichever of them the reciter recites, he is correct. The interpreters differed about the meaning of this. Some of them said: It means: He perfected and mastered everything. Who said that? Al-Abbas bin Abi Talib told me, he said: Al-Hussein bin Ibrahim Ishkab told us, he said: Sharik told us, on the authority of Khasif, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, Who has perfected everything which He created, he said: As for the monkey’s anus, it is not good, but He perfected its creation. Ibn Wakee’ told us: Abu Al-Nadr told us: Abu Saeed Al-Mu’addab told us, on the authority of Khasif, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, that he used to recite it: He who has perfected everything which He created. He said: As for the monkey’s anus, it is not good, but He perfected it. Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us both, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, He created everything in the best possible way, he said: He created everything perfectly. Muhammad bin Amara told me, he said: Abdullah bin Musa told us, he said: Israel told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid he mastered everything: he counted everything. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: He who created everything well. Who said that? Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, his statement, Who has perfected everything which He created, is good in the way in which He created. It was reported on the authority of Al-Hajjaj, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Al-A’raj, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: It is like He gave each thing its nature and form, then guided it (Ta-Ha 20:50). He said: So He did not make the creation of animals in the creation of people, nor the creation of people in the creation of animals, but He created each thing and determined it with a determination. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: He knows everything He created, as if they directed the interpretation of the statement to the fact that He inspired His creation with what they need, and that His saying best is only the saying of the speaker, So-and-so knows such-and-such well if he knows it. Who said that? Ibn Wakee’ told us: My father told us, on the authority of Sharik, on the authority of Khasif, on the authority of Mujahid: He created everything in the best possible way. He said: He gave everything its creation. He said: The human being is to the human being, “the horse is to the horse,” and the donkey is to the donkey. According to this statement, creation and all are in the accusative case because the best is applied to them. The first and most correct of the sayings in this regard, in my opinion, is the reading of those who read it as Who perfected everything He created with a fat-ha on the lam, and it is the saying of those who said: It means He perfected and perfected, because there is no meaning to it when it is read thus except for one of two ways: Either this which we said about the meaning of perfection and perfection, or the meaning of improvement which is in the meaning of beauty and goodness. So since there is in His creation that which is not doubted in its ugliness and vileness, it is known that He did not mean by it that He perfected everything He created, but rather that it means that He perfected it and perfected its craftsmanship. As for the other reading, which is with a sukoon on the lam, the most correct interpretation of it is the saying of those who said: The meaning of that is more general and He inspired everything He created, He is the best of them, as He said: Who gave to each thing its form and nature, then guided it (Ta-Ha: 50), because that is the most apparent of its meanings. As for those who interpreted it to mean: Who created everything perfect, they made creation an accusative in the sense of explanation, as if they said: Who created everything perfect from Himself. Some of them said: It is from the word al-muqaddam which means delay, and they explained that it is similar to the poet’s saying: He placed me with you in his arms for the night. I am the one who will do what he wants if he fears the enemy. Meaning: The night has placed me in your arms, and similar to what another said: As if Hind's teeth and her joy were the day we met on the slopes of Dabab As if Hind's teeth and her beauty. And His saying, And He began the creation of man from clay, God Almighty says: And He began the creation of Adam from clay.
